title: Earl Grey tea cake
subtitle: butter loaf cake steeped with Earl Grey tea
excerpt: Earl Grey tea cake infuses warm tea into the dried fruit before folding it into a butter sponge, giving the cake a floral bergamot flavour and a moist crumb. The tea-soaked fruit keeps the cake tender for several days. Steep the fruit for at least two hours, or overnight for the most pronounced flavour.
sourceNotes: British tea loaf tradition (documented in various 20th-century household baking manuals, public domain). The tea loaf and tea cake tradition referenced in Mrs Beeton (Book of Household Management, 1861, public domain).

recipe.freezeNotes: Slice and freeze for up to 2 months.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Soak the fruit in tea overnight for maximum flavour. The baked cake keeps well for 4 days in an airtight tin.

recipeTools.notes: 900 g (2 lb) loaf tin, greased and lined.

glossaryTerms.definition: Submerging dried fruit in liquid (here, hot tea) so it absorbs moisture and softens before baking. Soaking prevents the fruit from drawing moisture out of the surrounding batter during the bake and keeps the crumb tender. The longer the soak, the more liquid the fruit absorbs and the more pronounced the flavour of the soaking liquid becomes in the finished cake.

A pourable or spoonable mixture of flour, liquid, and fat that bakes into a cake or bread. Batter differs from dough in that it is too wet to knead. In a tea loaf, the batter is thick and dense, containing soaked fruit and egg, and firms up in the oven to a sliceable crumb.

content.text: Earl Grey tea cake is a dairy-free British loaf made by

dried fruit in strong hot tea until it swells. You get a dense, moist loaf that cuts cleanly and keeps well without butter or oil. The bergamot in Earl Grey carries through into the crumb, so use a good-quality tea with a clear floral scent.

items.prepNote: strong, freshly brewed and still hot

content.text: Brew 300 ml of strong Earl Grey tea. Put the dried fruit and soft brown sugar in a large bowl. Pour the hot tea over the fruit and stir to dissolve the sugar. Cover the bowl and leave to soak for at least 2 hours, or overnight in the refrigerator.
Heat the oven to 160 degrees Celsius (conventional). Grease and line a 900 g loaf tin with baking paper.
Beat the egg into the soaked fruit mixture. Sift in the self-raising flour and fold through with a large spoon until you have a thick, even
with no dry streaks of flour visible.

Spoon the batter into the prepared tin and level the surface. Bake for 55 to 65 minutes until the top is deep brown, the cake has pulled away from the sides, and a skewer pushed into the centre comes out clean.
Leave to cool in the tin for 15 minutes before turning out onto a cooling rack. The loaf slices best when fully cold.

attrs.avoid: Avoid stirring the batter vigorously after the flour is added.
attrs.fix: Fold the flour in gently with a large spoon or spatula. Overmixing develops gluten and tightens the crumb. The batter should look rough and thick, not smooth.

attrs.avoid: Avoid using fruit that has not fully absorbed the tea.
attrs.fix: Make sure the fruit has soaked for at least 2 hours. Most of the tea should be absorbed; if there is still liquid pooling at the bottom of the bowl after soaking, drain off the excess before adding the egg and flour.

attrs.problem: Skewer comes out wet but top looks done
attrs.avoid: Avoid removing the loaf from the oven before the skewer is clean.
attrs.fix: Cover the tin loosely with a sheet of baking paper and continue baking in 10-minute increments. This cake can take up to 70 minutes depending on the oven. A clean skewer and a firm centre are the only reliable tests.

attrs.problem: Bergamot flavour is faint in the finished loaf
attrs.avoid: Avoid using a weak tea or steeping the fruit for less than 2 hours.
attrs.fix: Brew the tea double-strength using 2 teabags per 300 ml and steep for 5 minutes before pouring over the fruit. Soak overnight in the refrigerator for the fullest flavour transfer.
